title: AI Avatars
readingMarkdown:
# AI Avatars

An AI avatar is a synthetic presenter: a face and upper body, generated or animated, that speaks whatever script it is given. Type a paragraph, and a person on screen says it, with moving lips, blinks, and nods, in any of dozens of languages.

For some work this is a real gain. A training video can be updated by editing its script. One presenter can address forty markets. Nobody needs a studio. For other work it backfires, because audiences read faces with great skill and react badly to one that is nearly right. And an avatar that looks like a real person is that person's likeness, with everything that follows from it. This chapter covers how talking heads are generated, the choice between a stock avatar and a twin of a real person, and where avatars help, where they hurt, and what must be disclosed.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### A ventriloquist's puppet, very well made

A ventriloquist's puppet has a face that moves in time with a voice that is not its own. The audience knows this and enjoys it, as long as the mouth moves when the words come.

An AI avatar is the same arrangement with better craft. There is a voice track, from the tools of Module 6.4. There is a face. And there is a system whose whole job is to move the face so that it appears to be producing the voice. If the lips close on every "b" and "m" and round on every "o", the illusion holds. If they drift by a tenth of a second, it collapses, and the viewer stops listening and starts watching the mouth.

Two things follow. The quality of an avatar video rests first on the voice and the script, which the avatar merely delivers. And the standard the audience applies is the one it applies to human faces, which is the most demanding standard there is.

### Two families

```text
   LIP SYNC ON REAL FOOTAGE                    GENERATED TALKING HEAD

   real video of a person                      one photograph, or a short video
   + new audio                                 + audio
        |                                           |
        v                                           v
   only the mouth region is redrawn            the whole head is generated:
   to match the new audio                      lips, expression, blinks, head motion

   the face is real, the words are new         nothing on screen was filmed
   used for dubbing and for digital twins      used for stock avatars and photo avatars
```

Commercial avatar tools combine the two. The important distinction for a user is the one at the bottom of each column: how much of what the viewer sees was ever filmed.

### Three kinds of avatar

| Kind | Made from | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| **Stock avatar** | Footage of a paid actor, licensed by the vendor | A presenter nobody knows |
| **Custom avatar, or digital twin** | A few minutes of footage of a specific person, with their consent | That person |
| **Photo or generated avatar** | A single image, real or AI-generated | Whoever is in the image, or nobody |

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### Lip sync

Speech is made of sounds called phonemes. Many phonemes look alike on the face: "p", "b", and "m" all close the lips. The visible mouth shapes are called **visemes**, and there are far fewer of them than there are phonemes.

| Mouth shape | Sounds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Lips closed | m, b, p | "mop" |
| Teeth on lip | f, v | "five" |
| Open | a | "father" |
| Wide | e, i | "see" |
| Rounded | o, u, w | "who" |
| Narrow | most other consonants | "tent" |
| Rest | silence | a pause |

Lip sync is the problem of producing the right viseme at the right moment. The closed-lip shapes matter most. A viewer forgives a vowel that is a little too open. A "b" with the lips apart is seen at once.

Older systems animated a face from rules like the table above. Modern ones learn the mapping from video. Wav2Lip, a 2020 system, trained a network to redraw the mouth region of existing footage to match new audio, and its key idea was to train against a second network that had learned to judge whether lips and sound belong together. Systems since then, such as Microsoft's VASA-1 in 2024, generate the whole head from a single photograph and an audio track, including expressions, blinks, and head movement, and do it fast enough for live use.

### How close is close enough?

Broadcasters have long measured how much mismatch between sound and picture viewers notice. A recommendation of the International Telecommunication Union gives the figures.

| Offset of the sound from the picture | Viewers |
|---|---|
| From 125 ms late to 45 ms early | Do not detect it |
| Up to 185 ms late or 90 ms early | Detect it |
| Beyond that | Find it unacceptable |

The window is not symmetric. In the physical world sound arrives after light, so people tolerate sound that is late much better than sound that is early.

If the audio is offset from the video by $\Delta$ milliseconds, positive when the sound leads, the test for going undetected is

$$
-125 \le \Delta \le 45
$$

For an avatar this sets the bar. Lips that move a tenth of a second ahead of the voice pass unnoticed. Lips that trail the voice by a tenth of a second do not.

### The uncanny valley

In 1970 the roboticist Masahiro Mori proposed that our liking for an artificial figure rises as it becomes more human-like, then drops sharply when it is almost but not quite human, and recovers only when it is indistinguishable. He called the drop the **uncanny valley**, and suggested that movement deepens it.

```text
   liking
     ^                                              real person
     |                               stylised           *
     |                 cartoon       character         /
     |    simple          *  *  *  *                   /
     |    robot      *                 *              /
     |      *                            *           /
     |  *                                  *        /
     +----------------------------------------*----/-----> human likeness
                                               \__/
                                         almost human:
                                         the uncanny valley
```

It remains a hypothesis and not a law, and studies of it give mixed results. As a working guide for avatar video it is sound. An avatar that is frankly stylised is judged as a cartoon. One that aims at realism is judged as a person, and every flaw counts against it: eyes that do not quite track, a smile that ends at the mouth, a head that sways on a fixed loop, teeth that shimmer.

The practical consequences are these. Keep a realistic avatar on screen in short stretches. Frame it at a distance that hides fine flaws. Or choose a stylised look and step out of the valley altogether.

### What audiences make of AI presenters

Research is recent, mostly from education, and the pattern so far is consistent enough to plan around. Studies comparing AI presenters with human ones have generally found similar learning: people remember about as much. They have also tended to find lower engagement and lower stated trust, and some report that viewers' attention rests more on a human presenter's face. Surveys of students report that many would not choose an AI presenter if offered a human one.

Read as guidance: an avatar can deliver information. It is weak at the things a human presence is for, namely warmth, credibility, and persuasion.

### Stock avatar or digital twin?

| | Stock avatar | Digital twin |
|---|---|---|
| Who it looks like | An actor licensed by the vendor | A specific real person |
| Set-up | None | Recording, consent, and processing |
| Consent needed from | Nobody, by you. The vendor holds the licence | The person, recorded and in writing |
| Recognised by your audience | No | Yes, if they know the person |
| Risk if misused | Low | High: words put in a real person's mouth |
| Suits | Generic explainers, internal training | A founder, a teacher, or a known presenter at scale |

A twin costs something to set up. The comparison with filming is simple arithmetic. If filming costs $F$ per video, an avatar costs $a$ per minute for videos of $m$ minutes, and the twin costs $S$ to create, the avatar is cheaper once the number of videos $n$ satisfies

$$
n > \frac{S}{F - a\,m}
$$

With set-up at USD 400, filming at USD 150 a video, and an avatar at USD 5 a minute for three-minute videos, the break-even is three videos. Translation multiplies the advantage: the same script in six languages is six avatar renders and no extra filming.

The formula compares costs only. It says nothing about whether the avatar video is as effective as the filmed one, which the evidence on audiences above suggests it may not be.

### Consent for a twin

A digital twin is the likeness of a real person, and often their voice. The reputable tools require proof of consent before creating one: typically a recording of the person stating that they agree. That is the vendor's protection. Yours should go further, because a recording says nothing about what the twin may be used for.

A consent record for a twin should state:

- who the person is, with the consent recording
- which uses are permitted
- when the permission ends
- how the person can withdraw, and what happens to the avatar when they do
- whether they approve each script, or only a category of content
- whether the voice is included, with separate consent for it

The fifth point is the one most often missed. A twin can be made to say anything. An employee who agreed to present safety training has not agreed to announce redundancies, endorse a product, or go on appearing after they have left the company.

### Disclosure and the law

Avatars sit at the centre of the rules described in Module 6.1.

**Labelling.** A realistic synthetic person is what platform disclosure rules are written for. The EU's AI Act requires those who deploy deepfake video to disclose that it is artificially generated. One large social platform now requires accounts that present an AI-generated person to carry a profile-level label, or lose reach.

**Impersonation.** In the United States, a rule of the Federal Trade Commission from 2024 prohibits impersonating businesses and government in commerce. An avatar made to resemble a real person, used without their consent, also runs into the laws protecting a person's likeness. Several countries are drafting laws aimed directly at digital replicas.

**Testimonials.** An avatar that says "I used this product and loved it" is a fabricated testimonial. Module 6.1 noted that consumer protection rules ban these, including when AI generates them. An avatar can present what a product does. It cannot have had an experience.

**Honesty with the audience.** The simplest rule covers most cases: do not let viewers believe they are watching a real person speak when they are not.

### Where avatars work

| Works | Backfires |
|---|---|
| Internal training and onboarding | Sales and anything asking for trust |
| Product how-to and support videos | Apologies, bad news, emotional subjects |
| Frequently updated material | A leader's personal message |
| The same content in many languages | Testimonials and reviews |
| Short explainer segments with cutaways | A long piece to camera |

### Making one that people will watch

The script comes first, and Module 6.4's rules for the ear apply in full. Beyond that:

- **Short stretches on screen.** Cut away to slides, screen recordings, or footage every few seconds. The avatar introduces and links. The cutaways carry the content.
- **Medium framing.** A head-and-shoulders shot is kinder than a close-up.
- **Captions.** Many viewers watch without sound, and captions draw the eye away from the mouth.
- **A good voice.** A flat voice makes any face look dead.
- **Check the closed-lip sounds.** Watch the "b", "m", and "p" sounds, and names and numbers, where sync errors show first.

### Complexity

Generating avatar video costs in proportion to its length, usually priced by the minute. Everything in the lab is linear in the length of the script. The real cost to weigh is the audience's attention, which a talking head spends faster than almost any other kind of shot.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

First, the sequence of mouth shapes, and the test for sync.

```python
SHAPES = {"closed": "mbp", "teeth": "fv", "open": "a", "wide": "ei", "round": "ouw"}

def viseme_sequence(text):
    track = []
    for character in text.lower():
        if character.isalpha():
            shape = next((name for name, letters in SHAPES.items() if character in letters), "narrow")
        elif character.isspace():
            shape = "rest"
        else:
            continue
        if not track or track[-1] != shape:
            track.append(shape)
    return track

def sync_check(offset_ms):
    if -125 <= offset_ms <= 45:
        return "in sync"
    if -185 <= offset_ms <= 90:
        return "noticeable"
    return "unacceptable"

print(viseme_sequence("mama"), viseme_sequence("Bob"), viseme_sequence("five"))
print(viseme_sequence("Flatten the back first."))
print([sync_check(offset) for offset in (0, 45, 46, 91, -100, -126, -186)])
```

- **`viseme_sequence` maps each letter to a mouth shape.** This is a deliberate simplification. Real systems work from the sounds in the audio, and English spelling is a poor guide to sound. The letters are enough to show the idea.
- **Repeated shapes are merged.** A mouth that is already closed does not close again, so consecutive identical shapes become one.
- **"mama" alternates closed and open.** "Bob" is closed, round, closed. "five" puts the teeth on the lip twice. These are the shapes a viewer checks without knowing it.
- **A spoken sentence is a rapid sequence.** "Flatten the back first" passes through seventeen shapes, with a rest between words. An avatar system has to hit each one at the right instant.
- **`sync_check` applies the broadcast thresholds.** A positive offset means the sound comes before the picture.
- **Sound 45 milliseconds early is in sync, and 46 is noticeable.** Beyond 90 it is unacceptable.
- **Sound that is late is tolerated far more.** 100 milliseconds late goes undetected. It takes 126 to be noticed and 186 to be unacceptable.

Next, planning the cutaways.

```python
def cutaway_plan(sentences, wpm=150, max_on_screen=8.0):
    plan, clock, on_screen = [], 0.0, 0.0
    for sentence in sentences:
        seconds = round(len(sentence.split()) / wpm * 60, 1)
        if on_screen > 0 and on_screen + seconds > max_on_screen:
            visual, on_screen = "b-roll", 0.0
        else:
            visual, on_screen = "avatar", on_screen + seconds
        plan.append({"start": round(clock, 1), "end": round(clock + seconds, 1), "visual": visual})
        clock += seconds
    return plan

SCRIPT = [
    "A blunt chisel tears the wood and leaves a rough surface that no amount of sanding will fix.",
    "You can put that right in about ten minutes with two stones and a strip of leather.",
    "Start on the coarse stone and keep the bevel flat against it.",
    "Count twenty strokes, then turn the blade over and take off the burr.",
    "Move to the fine stone and repeat with a lighter touch.",
    "Finish on the leather strop.",
    "The edge should now shave a thin curl from the end grain of a piece of pine.",
]
for row in cutaway_plan(SCRIPT):
    print(row["start"], row["end"], row["visual"])
```

- **Each sentence is timed at the speaking rate.** The duration is the number of words divided by words per minute, as in Module 6.4.
- **The function tracks how long the avatar has been on screen.** While adding the next sentence keeps that under the limit, the avatar stays.
- **When the next sentence would pass the limit, it is given to a cutaway.** The picture changes to supporting footage while the voice continues, and the avatar's time on screen is reset.
- **The first sentence is always the avatar.** A presenter should be seen before being heard over other pictures.
- **This script of 37 seconds has three cutaways.** The avatar is never on screen for more than about seven seconds at a stretch.
- **The cutaways fall where the script describes actions.** The sentences about the two stones and about counting twenty strokes are covered by footage of the stones and the strokes, which is what the viewer wanted to see anyway.

Then, the consent record.

```python
REQUIRED = ("person", "consent_recording", "permitted_uses", "expiry", "withdrawal_process", "script_approval")

def consent_gaps(record):
    gaps = [key for key in REQUIRED if not record.get(key)]
    if record.get("includes_voice") and not record.get("voice_consent"):
        gaps.append("voice_consent")
    return gaps

COMPLETE = {
    "person": "Priya Shah", "consent_recording": "consent-2026-11-02.mp4",
    "permitted_uses": ["training videos", "product tutorials"], "expiry": "2027-11-02",
    "withdrawal_process": "email to legal, removal within 14 days",
    "script_approval": "Priya approves every script", "includes_voice": True,
    "voice_consent": "consent-voice-2026-11-02.wav",
}
print(consent_gaps(COMPLETE))
print(consent_gaps({"person": "The founder", "includes_voice": True}))
```

- **Six items are required for any twin.** The person, the recording of their consent, the permitted uses, an end date, a way to withdraw, and who approves scripts.
- **A seventh applies when the voice is cloned too.** The voice needs its own consent, as Module 6.4 explained.
- **The complete record has no gaps.**
- **"The founder", with nothing else, has six.** There is a name and an intention. There is no consent, no scope, no end date, no way out, no control over what is said, and no permission for the voice.
- **The function checks that each item exists, not that it is adequate.** A permitted use of "anything" would pass. Reading the record is a person's job.

Finally, the cost against filming.

```python
def avatar_vs_filming(videos, minutes_each, languages, film_cost_per_video, avatar_cost_per_minute, avatar_setup=0):
    filming = videos * languages * film_cost_per_video
    avatar = avatar_setup + videos * languages * minutes_each * avatar_cost_per_minute
    return {"filming": round(filming, 2), "avatar": round(avatar, 2), "cheaper": "avatar" if avatar < filming else "filming"}

print(avatar_vs_filming(2, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400))
print(avatar_vs_filming(3, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400))
print(avatar_vs_filming(20, 3, 6, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400))
```

- **Filming is costed per video, and the avatar per minute, plus a one-off set-up.** Both are multiplied by the number of languages.
- **For two videos, filming is cheaper.** USD 300 against USD 430, because the set-up has not been recovered.
- **At three videos the avatar is just ahead.** USD 445 against USD 450, which is the break-even from Section 2.
- **For twenty videos in six languages the gap is very large.** USD 2,200 against USD 18,000. This is the case avatars were built for: volume and translation.
- **The model treats each language as a separate shoot.** In practice a filmed video would be dubbed or subtitled and not reshot, so the real gap is smaller. And the comparison is of cost alone. Whether the audience responds as well is a separate question, and it should be tested on a few videos before twenty are made.

**Complexity.** `viseme_sequence` is linear in the text. `cutaway_plan` is linear in the sentences. The other functions do a fixed amount of work.

### An avatar video brief

```text
PURPOSE:      [what the viewer should be able to do afterwards]
AUDIENCE:     [who, and do they know the person shown?]
AVATAR:       [stock: name and licence / twin of: ___, consent record: ___]
VOICE:        [stock / cloned with consent]            LANGUAGES: [list]
SCRIPT:       [words]  at 150 wpm = [seconds]          Approved by: [person shown, if a twin]
ON SCREEN:    avatar for at most [8] seconds at a time, cutaways listed against the script
CAPTIONS:     yes
DISCLOSURE:   [platform label set / "presented by an AI avatar" in the video or description]
CHECKED:      closed-lip sounds, names, numbers, eye line, hands, teeth
```

### Deciding whether to use an avatar at all

| Question | If yes |
|---|---|
| Is the content information more than persuasion? | An avatar can carry it |
| Will it be updated often, or translated? | An avatar saves real effort |
| Does the message depend on who is saying it? | Film the person |
| Is the subject sensitive or emotional? | Film the person |
| Would the audience feel deceived to learn it was synthetic? | Disclose clearly, or do not use one |
| Could a voiceover over footage do the job? | Do that. It avoids the face entirely |

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**A long piece to camera.** Two minutes of an avatar looking into the lens gives the viewer two minutes to study its flaws. Keep it to a few seconds at a time and let cutaways carry the content.

**Blaming the avatar for a bad script.** A wooden script delivered by a wooden face is twice as wooden. Most complaints about avatar video are complaints about writing meant for the page.

**A flat voice.** The face is animated from the voice. A monotone voice produces a nearly motionless face. Fix the voice first.

**Fast speech.** Lip sync degrades as the speaking rate rises. Slow the delivery, shorten the sentences, and add pauses.

**Names and numbers.** These are where the voice mispronounces and where the lips are most visibly wrong. Check each one.

**Hands and gestures.** Many avatars loop a small set of movements. Once a viewer notices the loop, they see nothing else. Frame tighter or cut away sooner.

**Teeth and the inside of the mouth.** These remain the commonest artefact: teeth that shift or blur. A medium shot hides more than a close-up.

**A poor recording for a twin.** Bad lighting, a busy background, or a subject who barely moves gives a poor twin. Record evenly lit, on a plain background, with natural gestures and pauses.

**Using a twin for sales.** Prospects who discover that the personal video from the account manager was generated tend to feel deceived. Where trust is the point, film the person, or say plainly that it is an avatar.

**No written consent.** "She said it was fine" is not a record. Staff leave, relationships sour, and a twin can say anything. Write down the uses, the end date, and how to withdraw.

**A twin that outlives the job.** An avatar of an employee who has left is still presenting the training. Tie the permission to a date and a process for removal.

**Fabricated testimonials.** An avatar "customer" praising the product is a fake review whatever disclaimer follows. Do not make them.

**No disclosure.** A realistic avatar presented as a real person risks platform penalties and, more lastingly, the audience's trust. Label it.

**Reaching for an avatar by default.** Often a voice over screen recordings or footage is clearer, cheaper, and free of the uncanny valley. Ask whether a face is needed at all.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** An AI avatar is a face animated to match a voice track. Lip sync means producing the right mouth shape, or viseme, at the right moment, with the closed-lip sounds mattering most, and viewers detect sound that leads the picture by more than about 45 milliseconds or trails it by more than about 125. Because a realistic avatar is judged as a human face, small flaws are costly, which is the practical content of the uncanny valley: use short stretches on screen, medium framing, cutaways, and captions, or choose a stylised look. Evidence so far suggests avatars convey information about as well as people and do less well on engagement and trust, so they suit training, how-to, frequently updated, and translated content, and suit persuasion and emotional subjects badly. A stock avatar needs no consent from you. A digital twin needs the person's recorded and written consent covering permitted uses, an end date, withdrawal, script approval, and the voice. A twin is cheaper than filming once the number of videos passes $S/(F - am)$. Realistic synthetic presenters must be disclosed, must not impersonate anyone, and cannot give testimonials.

**Question 1.** Creating a digital twin costs USD 600. Filming a four-minute video costs USD 200, and the avatar tool charges USD 6 per minute. After how many videos is the avatar cheaper? The company plans 15 videos in 5 languages. Compare the totals as the simple model computes them, and say what the model leaves out.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

An avatar video of four minutes costs 4 times 6, which is USD 24. Filming costs USD 200, so each video made with the avatar saves USD 176. The set-up of USD 600 is recovered after 600 divided by 176, which is about 3.4, so the avatar is cheaper from the fourth video. For 15 videos in 5 languages, the simple model counts 75 productions. Filming is 75 times 200, which is USD 15,000. The avatar is 600 plus 75 times 24, which is 600 plus 1,800, or USD 2,400. The avatar is cheaper by USD 12,600. The model leaves out several things. It assumes each language would be filmed separately, when in practice a filmed video would be dubbed or subtitled for far less, so the true saving is smaller. It ignores the cost of translation and of checking the translated scripts, which both routes need. It ignores the time to write scripts for the ear, to plan and produce the cutaways, and to check lip sync on every render. It ignores the work of consent: recording it, agreeing its scope, and reviewing scripts with the person shown. Most of all, it compares cost and not effect. If viewers engage less with an avatar or trust it less, cheaper videos that work less well may be the more expensive choice. The sensible course is to make three or four videos both ways, measure completion and comprehension, and decide after that.

</details>

**Question 2.** A reviewer measures three avatar clips. In the first the sound is 30 milliseconds ahead of the lips. In the second it is 110 milliseconds behind. In the third it is 70 milliseconds ahead. Which will viewers notice, and why are early and late sound treated so differently? What else, apart from timing, would you check about the mouth?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Using the broadcast thresholds, viewers do not detect an offset between 125 milliseconds late and 45 milliseconds early. The first clip, with sound 30 milliseconds early, is inside that window and will pass. The second, with sound 110 milliseconds late, is also inside it and will pass, although it is the largest offset of the three. The third, with sound 70 milliseconds early, is outside the window of 45 and inside the limit of 90, so viewers will notice it, though it is short of the level judged unacceptable. So only the third is a problem, and its offset is smaller than the second's. The asymmetry comes from ordinary experience. Light travels much faster than sound, so in the physical world the sight of an event always arrives before its sound, slightly for a person across a room and obviously for a distant hammer. People are therefore used to sound that lags and adapt to it without effort. Sound that arrives before the lips move never happens naturally, so the mismatch is caught at a much smaller offset. For avatars, the rule is that if there must be an error, the lips should lead and never trail the voice. Beyond timing, the mouth shapes themselves need checking. The lips must actually close on the "b", "m", and "p" sounds, since an open mouth on those is seen immediately. The teeth and the inside of the mouth should be stable and not shimmer. Names and numbers deserve a look, since mispronunciations and sync errors cluster there, and so do fast passages, where sync degrades. And the rest of the face should agree with the speech, with the expression matching the tone and blinks and head movement that do not visibly loop.

</details>

**Question 3.** A company created a digital twin of a popular trainer for its onboarding videos, with her agreement given in a recorded statement. A year later she has left the company. Marketing now wants to use the twin in an advertisement in which "she" says the product changed her career. Identify every problem and say what the original consent record should have contained.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

There are four problems. The first is scope. She agreed to present onboarding videos. An advertisement is a different use, commercial and public, and nothing in a general statement of agreement extends to it. Using a person's likeness to sell something without their consent to that use is what laws protecting likeness are aimed at. The second is that she has left. Consent given as an employee, for the employer's training, does not obviously survive the end of the employment, and continuing to use the twin at all, even for onboarding, is questionable without an agreement that says so. The third is the content. The advertisement has her say that the product changed her career. That is a statement of personal experience, which she never made, put in her mouth by the company. It is a fabricated testimonial, prohibited by consumer protection rules whether or not AI is involved, and it is a false statement attributed to a real, identifiable person, which exposes the company to her claims as well as to regulators'. The fourth is disclosure. A realistic synthetic video of a real person is what platform rules and the EU's transparency rules require to be labelled, and a label would not cure the first three problems. The original record should have named her, with the consent recording, and listed the permitted uses specifically, here internal onboarding videos only. It should have set an end date, and said what happens on her leaving the company, with a process for withdrawal and removal of the avatar within a stated time. It should have given her approval of each script, or of a defined category of content. And it should have covered her voice with separate consent. With that record, marketing's request would have been answered by reading it. The right course now is to stop, and, if the company wants her in an advertisement, to ask her, pay her, and film her saying only what she is willing to say.

</details>

interactiveLab.context: A woodworking shop is deciding whether to present its training videos with an AI avatar of its lead instructor. You will build the sequence of mouth shapes behind lip sync, a check of whether sound and picture are in step, a plan for cutting away from the avatar before it outstays its welcome, a check of a consent record, and a comparison of the cost of an avatar with the cost of filming.
interactiveLab.starterCode:

    "permitted_uses": ["training videos", "product tutorials"], "expiry": "2027-11-02",
    "withdrawal_process": "email to legal, removal within 14 days",

    print("sync    :", sync_check(70))
    print("cutaways:", cutaway_plan(SCRIPT[:3]))

    print("cost    :", avatar_vs_filming(20, 3, 6, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400))

steps.title: The sequence of mouth shapes
steps.instruction: Implement viseme_sequence(text). Go through the lowercase text one character at a time. For a letter, the shape is the name in SHAPES whose string of letters contains it, or 'narrow' if none does. For white space the shape is 'rest'. Any other character, such as punctuation or a digit, is skipped. Add each shape to a list only if it differs from the last shape added, so that consecutive identical shapes are merged. Return the list. Try 'mama', 'Bob', and 'five'. This is the viseme table from Section 2, applied to spelling as a simplification. [MOD-6.5]
steps.hintConceptual: Watch someone say a word with the sound off. You do not see letters. You see the lips close, open, round, and pull wide, and a shape that is held does not happen twice.
steps.testAssertion:
assert viseme_sequence("mama") == ["closed", "open", "closed", "open"], f"'mama' alternates closed and open, got {viseme_sequence('mama')}"
assert viseme_sequence("Bob") == ["closed", "round", "closed"] and viseme_sequence("five") == ["teeth", "wide", "teeth", "wide"], "Capitals are treated as lowercase, and 'f' and 'v' put the teeth on the lip"
assert viseme_sequence("Flatten the back first.") == ["teeth", "narrow", "open", "narrow", "wide", "narrow", "rest", "narrow", "wide", "rest", "closed", "open", "narrow", "rest", "teeth", "wide", "narrow"], "A sentence, with a rest between words and the full stop skipped"
assert viseme_sequence("Hmm!") == ["narrow", "closed"], "Repeated shapes are merged, and punctuation is skipped"
assert viseme_sequence("a  a") == ["open", "rest", "open"], "Several spaces are one rest"
assert viseme_sequence("tent") == ["narrow", "wide", "narrow"] and viseme_sequence("who") == ["round", "narrow", "round"], "Most consonants are 'narrow', and 'w', 'o', and 'u' are 'round'"
assert viseme_sequence("") == [] and viseme_sequence("123 !?") == ["rest"], "Empty text has no shapes, and digits and punctuation are skipped"
print("Step 1 passed: 'mama' is closed, open, closed, open, and those are the shapes a viewer checks.")

steps.title: Is the sound in step with the picture?
steps.instruction: Implement sync_check(offset_ms). The offset is how far the sound leads the picture, in milliseconds: positive when the sound is early, negative when it is late. Return 'in sync' if the offset is between minus 125 and 45 inclusive. Otherwise return 'noticeable' if it is between minus 185 and 90 inclusive. Otherwise return 'unacceptable'. Check offsets of 30, minus 110, and 70. These are the broadcast thresholds from Section 2, and the window is not symmetric: late sound is tolerated much more than early sound. [MOD-6.5]
steps.hintConceptual: Thunder after lightning seems natural. Thunder before lightning would be alarming. The ear expects sound to trail the sight of its cause, never to run ahead of it.
steps.testAssertion:
assert sync_check(0) == "in sync" and sync_check(30) == "in sync" and sync_check(-110) == "in sync", f"Small offsets, and sound up to 125 ms late, go undetected, got {sync_check(-110)}"
assert sync_check(45) == "in sync" and sync_check(46) == "noticeable", "Sound more than 45 ms early is noticed"
assert sync_check(70) == "noticeable" and sync_check(90) == "noticeable" and sync_check(91) == "unacceptable", "Sound more than 90 ms early is unacceptable"
assert sync_check(-125) == "in sync" and sync_check(-126) == "noticeable", "Sound more than 125 ms late is noticed"
assert sync_check(-185) == "noticeable" and sync_check(-186) == "unacceptable", "Sound more than 185 ms late is unacceptable"
assert sync_check(-110) == "in sync" and sync_check(70) == "noticeable", "The window is not symmetric: 110 ms late passes and 70 ms early does not"
assert sync_check(1000) == "unacceptable" and sync_check(-1000) == "unacceptable", "Large offsets in either direction"
print("Step 2 passed: sound 110 ms late goes unnoticed, and sound 70 ms early does not.")

steps.title: Plan the cutaways
steps.instruction: Implement cutaway_plan(sentences, wpm, max_on_screen). Keep a clock and the avatar's current time on screen, both starting at 0.0. For each sentence, its duration in seconds is the number of words divided by wpm, times 60, rounded to 1 decimal place. If the avatar has already been on screen, meaning its time is above zero, and adding this sentence would take that time above max_on_screen, then this sentence is shown as 'b-roll' and the avatar's time resets to 0.0. Otherwise it is shown as 'avatar' and its time grows by the sentence's duration. Record a dict with 'start', the clock rounded to 1 place; 'end', the clock plus the duration, rounded to 1 place; and 'visual'. Then advance the clock by the duration. Return the list. Plan SCRIPT and count the cutaways. This is the advice of Section 2: short stretches on screen. [MOD-6.5]
steps.hintConceptual: A television interview cuts away from the speaker every few seconds, to the thing being described or to the listener. The voice carries on. The picture gives the eye somewhere else to go.
steps.testAssertion:
_plan = cutaway_plan(SCRIPT)
assert _plan is not None and [row["visual"] for row in _plan] == ["avatar", "b-roll", "avatar", "b-roll", "avatar", "avatar", "b-roll"], f"Seven sentences with three cutaways, got {_plan}"
assert _plan[0] == {"start": 0.0, "end": 7.2, "visual": "avatar"} and _plan[1] == {"start": 7.2, "end": 14.0, "visual": "b-roll"}, "The first sentence shows the avatar, and the second, which would take it past 8 seconds, cuts away"
assert _plan[-1]["end"] == 37.2 and [row["start"] for row in _plan] == [0.0, 7.2, 14.0, 18.8, 24.0, 28.4, 30.4], "The clock runs on through the cutaways, to 37.2 seconds"
assert _plan[4]["visual"] == "avatar" and _plan[5]["visual"] == "avatar", "Two short sentences, 4.4 and 2.0 seconds, fit in one stretch on screen"
_long = cutaway_plan(["word " * 30])
assert _long == [{"start": 0.0, "end": 12.0, "visual": "avatar"}], "The first sentence always shows the avatar, even when it is longer than the limit"
assert [row["visual"] for row in cutaway_plan(SCRIPT, max_on_screen=100)] == ["avatar"] * 7, "With a generous limit there are no cutaways"
assert [row["visual"] for row in cutaway_plan(SCRIPT, wpm=300)] == ["avatar", "avatar", "b-roll", "avatar", "avatar", "avatar", "b-roll"], "The speaking rate is an argument, and faster speech means fewer cutaways"
assert cutaway_plan([]) == [], "No sentences, no plan"
print("Step 3 passed: the avatar is never on screen for more than about seven seconds at a stretch.")

steps.title: Check a consent record
steps.instruction: Implement consent_gaps(record). Return a list of the keys in REQUIRED, in order, that are missing from the record or have an empty value. Then, if the record's 'includes_voice' is true and its 'voice_consent' is missing or empty, append 'voice_consent'. Run it on COMPLETE and on a record that has only a person and includes_voice. This is the list for a digital twin in Section 2. The function checks that each item is present. Whether a permitted use of 'anything' is acceptable is for a person to judge. [MOD-6.5]
steps.hintConceptual: A release form has boxes for who, what for, until when, how to cancel, and who signs off the words. A form with only a name on it is not a release.
steps.hintSyntax:
gaps = [key for key in REQUIRED if not record.get(key)]
if record.get("includes_voice") and not record.get("voice_consent"):
    gaps.append("voice_consent")
return gaps
steps.testAssertion:
assert consent_gaps(COMPLETE) == [], f"The complete record has no gaps, got {consent_gaps(COMPLETE)}"
assert consent_gaps({"person": "The founder", "includes_voice": True}) == ["consent_recording", "permitted_uses", "expiry", "withdrawal_process", "script_approval", "voice_consent"], "A name and an intention leave six gaps"
assert consent_gaps({}) == ["person", "consent_recording", "permitted_uses", "expiry", "withdrawal_process", "script_approval"], "An empty record is missing all six required items, and no voice consent is asked for when the voice is not included"
_no_voice = {key: value for key, value in COMPLETE.items() if key != "voice_consent"}
assert consent_gaps(_no_voice) == ["voice_consent"], "A twin that includes the voice needs separate consent for it"
assert consent_gaps(dict(_no_voice, includes_voice=False)) == [], "A silent twin, voiced by someone else, needs no voice consent"
assert consent_gaps(dict(COMPLETE, permitted_uses=[], expiry="")) == ["permitted_uses", "expiry"], "An empty list or an empty string counts as missing, and gaps are listed in the order of REQUIRED"
assert consent_gaps(dict(COMPLETE, permitted_uses=["anything"])) == [], "The function checks presence, not adequacy: 'anything' passes, and a person must read the record"
print("Step 4 passed: a twin needs recorded consent, a scope, an end date, a way out, script approval, and voice consent.")

steps.title: Compare the cost with filming
steps.instruction: Implement avatar_vs_filming(videos, minutes_each, languages, film_cost_per_video, avatar_cost_per_minute, avatar_setup). The cost of filming is the number of videos times the number of languages times the cost of filming one video. The cost of the avatar is the set-up cost plus the number of videos times the languages times the minutes of each video times the avatar's cost per minute. Return a dict with 'filming' and 'avatar', each rounded to 2 decimal places, and 'cheaper', which is 'avatar' if the avatar's cost is strictly less than filming and 'filming' otherwise. Compare 2 videos, then 3, then 20 videos in 6 languages, at USD 150 per filmed video, USD 5 per avatar minute, three minutes each, and a set-up of USD 400. This is the break-even from Section 2. [MOD-6.5]
steps.hintConceptual: A machine that costs a lot to install and little to run beats hand work only after enough pieces. Count the pieces before buying the machine.
steps.testAssertion:
assert avatar_vs_filming(2, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400) == {"filming": 300, "avatar": 430, "cheaper": "filming"}, f"For two videos the set-up is not recovered, got {avatar_vs_filming(2, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400)}"
assert avatar_vs_filming(3, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400) == {"filming": 450, "avatar": 445, "cheaper": "avatar"}, "At three videos the avatar is just ahead"
assert avatar_vs_filming(20, 3, 6, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400) == {"filming": 18000, "avatar": 2200, "cheaper": "avatar"}, "Twenty videos in six languages: USD 2,200 against USD 18,000"
assert avatar_vs_filming(15, 4, 5, 200, 6, avatar_setup=600) == {"filming": 15000, "avatar": 2400, "cheaper": "avatar"}, "The numbers from the first recall question"
assert avatar_vs_filming(1, 2, 1, 10, 5) == {"filming": 10, "avatar": 10, "cheaper": "filming"}, "With no set-up by default, and equal costs, filming is reported: the avatar must be strictly cheaper"
assert avatar_vs_filming(0, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400) == {"filming": 0, "avatar": 400, "cheaper": "filming"}, "With no videos, only the set-up has been spent"
assert avatar_vs_filming(4, 2.5, 1, 99.99, 3.333) == {"filming": 399.96, "avatar": 33.33, "cheaper": "avatar"}, "Costs are rounded to 2 places"
print("Step 5 passed: the avatar pays for itself at three videos, and translation multiplies the saving.")

interactiveLab.solutionCode:
"""
Lab solution: Mouth Shapes, Sync, Cutaways, Consent, and Cost
Standard library only.
"""

# Mouth shapes (visemes) and the letters that stand in for their sounds. A simplification:
# real systems work from the sounds in the audio, not from spelling.
SHAPES = {"closed": "mbp", "teeth": "fv", "open": "a", "wide": "ei", "round": "ouw"}

SCRIPT = [
    "A blunt chisel tears the wood and leaves a rough surface that no amount of sanding will fix.",
    "You can put that right in about ten minutes with two stones and a strip of leather.",
    "Start on the coarse stone and keep the bevel flat against it.",
    "Count twenty strokes, then turn the blade over and take off the burr.",
    "Move to the fine stone and repeat with a lighter touch.",
    "Finish on the leather strop.",
    "The edge should now shave a thin curl from the end grain of a piece of pine.",
]

REQUIRED = ("person", "consent_recording", "permitted_uses", "expiry", "withdrawal_process", "script_approval")

COMPLETE = {
    "person": "Priya Shah", "consent_recording": "consent-2026-11-02.mp4",
    "permitted_uses": ["training videos", "product tutorials"], "expiry": "2027-11-02",
    "withdrawal_process": "email to legal, removal within 14 days",
    "script_approval": "Priya approves every script", "includes_voice": True,
    "voice_consent": "consent-voice-2026-11-02.wav",
}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1
def viseme_sequence(text):
    """Lip sync is the right mouth shape at the right moment. The closed-lip shapes matter
    most: a viewer forgives a vowel and notices at once a 'b' with the lips apart."""
    track = []
    for character in text.lower():
        if character.isalpha():
            shape = next((name for name, letters in SHAPES.items() if character in letters), "narrow")
        elif character.isspace():
            shape = "rest"
        else:
            continue
        if not track or track[-1] != shape:
            track.append(shape)
    return track


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2
def sync_check(offset_ms):
    """The window is not symmetric. In the physical world sound arrives after light, so
    late sound is tolerated and early sound is not."""
    if -125 <= offset_ms <= 45:
        return "in sync"
    if -185 <= offset_ms <= 90:
        return "noticeable"
    return "unacceptable"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3
def cutaway_plan(sentences, wpm=150, max_on_screen=8.0):
    """A realistic face is judged as a person, and every second on screen is a chance to
    find a flaw. The avatar introduces and links. The cutaways carry the content."""
    plan, clock, on_screen = [], 0.0, 0.0
    for sentence in sentences:
        seconds = round(len(sentence.split()) / wpm * 60, 1)
        if on_screen > 0 and on_screen + seconds > max_on_screen:
            visual, on_screen = "b-roll", 0.0
        else:
            visual, on_screen = "avatar", on_screen + seconds
        plan.append({"start": round(clock, 1), "end": round(clock + seconds, 1), "visual": visual})
        clock += seconds
    return plan


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4
def consent_gaps(record):
    """A twin can be made to say anything, so consent has to say what it may be used for,
    until when, who approves the words, and how the person gets out."""
    gaps = [key for key in REQUIRED if not record.get(key)]
    if record.get("includes_voice") and not record.get("voice_consent"):
        gaps.append("voice_consent")
    return gaps


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5
def avatar_vs_filming(videos, minutes_each, languages, film_cost_per_video, avatar_cost_per_minute, avatar_setup=0):
    """A comparison of cost alone. Whether the audience responds as well to the avatar is a
    separate question, to be tested before the saving is counted."""
    filming = videos * languages * film_cost_per_video
    avatar = avatar_setup + videos * languages * minutes_each * avatar_cost_per_minute
    return {"filming": round(filming, 2), "avatar": round(avatar, 2), "cheaper": "avatar" if avatar < filming else "filming"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(viseme_sequence("mama"), viseme_sequence("Bob"), viseme_sequence("five"))
    print(viseme_sequence("Flatten the back first."), len(viseme_sequence("Flatten the back first.")))
    print([sync_check(offset) for offset in (0, 45, 46, 91, -100, -126, -186)])
    print(sync_check(30), sync_check(-110), sync_check(70))

    plan = cutaway_plan(SCRIPT)
    for row in plan:
        print(row["start"], row["end"], row["visual"])
    print(sum(1 for row in plan if row["visual"] == "b-roll"), plan[-1]["end"])

    print(consent_gaps(COMPLETE))
    print(consent_gaps({"person": "The founder", "includes_voice": True}))

    print(avatar_vs_filming(2, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400))
    print(avatar_vs_filming(3, 3, 1, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400))
    print(avatar_vs_filming(20, 3, 6, 150, 5, avatar_setup=400))
    print(round(400 / (150 - 3 * 5), 2), round(600 / (200 - 4 * 6), 2), avatar_vs_filming(15, 4, 5, 200, 6, avatar_setup=600))
